name: Yellow Tan
lede: Yellow Tan is a bright, warm yellow catalogued twice over in Ridgway's 1912 atlas, and a name whose printed use peaked decades after painters stopped reaching for the color.

sections.title: Catalogued twice
sections.body: Ridgway's 1912 systematic nomenclature places the hue on two separate plates, plate XVI (hue 23', tone b) and plate IV (hue 23, tone b), filed by the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 as two neighboring blocks, 86 and 101 [1]. The nearest named neighbor by measured color is [[pinard-yellow]], barely cooler [2]. In printed English, the phrase "yellow tan" itself rose fastest in the 1930s and peaked in the 1960s, in Google's scanned-book count of all senses of the words, which can mean the object or the place as easily as the color [3]. Further out, [[dull-yellow]] and [[gamboge-yellow]] sit in the same small cluster [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a match for Yellow Tan in only 46 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.2 percent, rarer than 52 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 6 of 945 paintings, 2.7 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 49 percent of its appearances [3]. The earliest match, from 1434, is a painting by Fra Angelico, nearly five centuries before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[3].

ngram.caveat: all senses of the words, not isolated to the color
